name: Usnea (old man's beard)
habitat: Hanging from the branches of trees in clean, humid air — conifers especially. It is an air-quality indicator and will not grow where pollution is heavy.
identify: Pale grey-green, shrubby or hair-like lichen hanging from bark.
THE TEST: gently pull a strand apart. Usnea has a white ELASTIC CORD running through the centre, like a tiny bungee inside the sheath. Nothing else does.
Dry and brittle when dry, softening and going rubbery when wet.

lookalikes.name: Spanish moss
lookalikes.danger: Not toxic, but it is a flowering plant, not a lichen, and has none of the usnic acid.
lookalikes.tell: No white inner cord; it is uniformly grey and scaly and grows mainly on southern US oaks and cypress.

lookalikes.name: Alectoria, Bryoria and other beard lichens
lookalikes.danger: Some, such as Bryoria tortuosa, carry vulpinic acid and are toxic.
lookalikes.tell: Again the cord test: pull a strand. No white elastic core means it is not Usnea. Bryoria is typically brown to black rather than grey-green.

preparations.method: Pack dried, clean lichen against a wound inside a cloth barrier.
preparations.for_use: An absorbent, mildly antiseptic field dressing.

preparations.method: Usnic acid is barely water-soluble — simmer long and hot for a weak wash, or extract properly in strong alcohol over weeks.
preparations.for_use: A wash for skin infections and fungal complaints. A water infusion is much weaker than a tincture.

cautions: Concentrated usnic acid taken INTERNALLY has caused severe liver injury, including fatalities from weight-loss supplements. Do not eat it or take concentrated extracts.
Lichens accumulate heavy metals and fallout from the air over decades. Do not gather near roads, industry, or known contamination.
Take fallen material after wind rather than stripping living lichen; it grows a few millimetres a year.
evidence: Usnic acid has well-documented in-vitro antibacterial activity, particularly against gram-positive bacteria. Topical traditional use is long-standing; internal use is genuinely dangerous.
